title: Print root to leaf path in BT
statement:
Given the root of a binary tree. Return all the **root-to-leaf paths** in the binary tree.

A leaf node of a binary tree is the node which does not have a left and right child.

**Example 1:**

```
Input : root = [1, 2, 3, null, 5, null, 4]
Output : [ [1, 2, 5] , [1, 3, 4] ]
Explanation : There are only two paths from root to leaf.
From root 1 to 5 , 1 -> 2 -> 5.
From root 1 to 4 , 1 -> 3 -> 4.
![](https://static.takeuforward.org/content/1789463410_b7JrBMOo.webp)
```

**Example 2:**

```
Input : root = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
Output : [ [1, 2, 4] , [1, 2, 5] , [1, 3] ]
Explanation :
![](https://static.takeuforward.org/content/1789463418_cNvpTMB7.webp)
```

hints.title: Hint 1
hints.body: Start from the root node and traverse the tree recursively. Maintain a current path list that stores nodes visited so far.

hints.title: Hint 2
hints.body: When reaching a leaf node, store the current path in the result list. Use backtracking to remove the last node when returning from recursion.

doubts.question: Why use DFS instead of BFS?
doubts.answer: DFS is naturally suited for pathfinding problems since it explores one complete path before backtracking. BFS requires storing more nodes in memory, making it less space-efficient.

doubts.question: Why do we need backtracking in the recursive approach?
doubts.answer: When returning from recursion, we remove the last node from the path to ensure it does not affect other recursive calls.

followUps.question: What if we needed to return paths as strings instead of lists?
followUps.answer: Instead of storing lists, concatenate values into a string like "1->2->5".

followUps.question: What if some nodes had a special property (e.g., sum constraint)?
followUps.answer: Modify traversal to include a running sum and filter paths based on conditions.
